The 28 tram climbs through Alfama on rails laid before cars existed here, and half the tourists riding it are filming instead of looking out the window. Skip it during the day. Ride it at 8pm instead, when the crowds have thinned and the yellow paint catches the last light off the tile facades.

Lisbon works as a weekend trip because the city is compact enough to walk and steep enough that you'll want the miradouros as excuses to stop. Miradouro de Santa Luzia, just below the castle, has a wall of blue-and-white azulejos depicting the 1147 siege and a view over the Alfama rooftops to the river. Get there before 10am or after 6pm — midday brings tour groups with flags.

Breakfast should be a pastel de nata, eaten standing up, from wherever is closest: Manteigaria in Chiado if you want the version with the burnt sugar top, or any neighborhood padaria if you don't want to wait in line. The Belém original is worth one visit for the recipe's history, not because it's meaningfully better than the copies.

Spend Saturday afternoon at LX Factory, an old textile complex under the 25 de Abril bridge, now full of bookshops and print studios. The Ler Devagar bookstore has a bicycle sculpture suspended from the ceiling and enough English-language stock to spend an hour browsing. Walk down to the river after. The bridge looks almost exactly like the Golden Gate because the same American firm, USACE, engineered both.

Dinner is where the city stops being photogenic and starts being good. Cervejaria Ramiro, if you can get a table, does percebes — goose barnacles that look unsettling and taste like the ocean reduced to a single bite. If the wait is too long, any tasca in Bica will do grilled sardines and a jug of house vinho verde for under 15 euros.

Sunday morning, take the ferry across to Cacilhas instead of squeezing in another museum. It costs about a euro, takes ten minutes, and hands you the skyline view every postcard in the city is trying to sell — minus the postcard price. From the far bank, Lisbon looks smaller than it feels from inside it: a compact grid of red roofs climbing seven hills, with the castle sitting slightly crooked at the top.
